articles.title: UK considers regulating AI if voluntary safeguards prove insufficient
articles.description: The United Kingdom is considering regulating advanced AI models if the current voluntary system of pre-implementation testing proves insufficient to protect the public, AI Minister Kanishka Narayan told Reuters. The UK has favored a lighter approach to AI regulation, aligning more with the United States than the European Union, whose AI Act came into effect on Sunday (2nd). Read more: US finalizes voluntary AI safety tests, White House official says The government sees AI as an economic growth driver and has sought to position the UK as a leading global destination for AI investment. In Europe, the country leads in funding and the number of AI startups. Uncontrolled AI agents But recent disclosures from AI companies have reignited the debate about the need to strengthen oversight of so-called frontier models. Anthropic reported on Thursday (30th) that some Claude models had breached the systems of three companies during cybersecurity tests, just days after OpenAI revealed that one of its AI agents had gone out of control. The UK's AI Safety Institute, established after the 2023 AI Safety Summit, receives early access to AI model implementations through voluntary agreements with OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, and other companies, allowing it to assess their capabilities and risks. Narayan, promoted to the cabinet by new Prime Minister Andy Burnham, stated that this access gives the UK a privileged view into frontier AI development. 'If the right mechanism and tool change over time and it appears that regulation might be a way to help us do that, then of course we will look at it,' he said in an interview. He stated that the institute has early access to the implementation of almost all frontier AI models developed by Western companies, making the UK the only country besides the United States with this level of access. 'This is really something very, very unique,' the minister said. Narayan stated that the government's priority is to protect the public and that it is focused on outcomes, not on 'just sticking to the mechanism.' The UK has not created a dedicated AI regulator, opting to rely on existing authorities responsible for areas such as competition, human rights, and health and safety. When asked about AI last week, US President Donald Trump said his administration was 'looking at controls' but added that he did not want to jeopardize the country's leadership in AI. Unsplash

articles.title: Sem (22) is world champion Stratego: 'No one can take this away from me anymore'
articles.description: Sem van Geffen (22) from Eerde became world champion Stratego last weekend in Leiden. It is the first time he has won the world title. His brother and father have preceded him. 'And now I have taken over the baton.' The general, marshal, and the bomb. Anyone who has played the game Stratego before will remember these ranks. In Stratego, two armies, consisting of different pawns each with their own rank, battle each other. The goal is to find the opponent's flag. And Sem found that flag often enough during the World Championship. And Sem is not the only one in the family who is so good at the game. 'My father Johnny became champion in 1999 and my brother Vince won three times in a row in recent years. And now I have taken over the baton from him.' Sem and Vince learned the game from their father. And father Johnny learned it from 'master Wim'. 'Our dad met Wim at a Stratego tournament and he taught my father. Wim plays a very important role for us. He was also there this weekend.' And what makes Stratego such an interesting game? 'You can determine your own setup. In chess, there is a fixed setup and everything is visible. In Stratego, it is not visible what an opponent has placed,' Sem explains. 'Personally, I find it more difficult than chess, because you can think six or seven steps ahead.' The World Championship is a great victory for Sem. 'I have reached my goal and no one can take this away from me anymore,' he says. Although he won't be busy moving game pieces for the next few days. 'It's been enough after two days and ten games. I'm going to enjoy it first!'

articles.title: White House to host meeting on new AI review regime
articles.description: WASHINGTON, United States — The White House will host a meeting Tuesday with AI executives to discuss a new voluntary system of government review of the technology's most powerful models, an administration official said. The official did not specify who will attend the discussions on the new regulatory regime outlined in an executive order that President Donald Trump signed on June 2. The central provision of this framework allows companies such as OpenAI, Google or Anthropic to give the government access to their most powerful models for up to 30 days before planned release to the general public. The order was triggered by concerns over Anthropic's Mythos model, which the AI startup initially refused to release publicly due to its ability to expose vulnerabilities in computer systems, including those of banks, governments and hospitals. Mythos was eventually released, albeit with restrictions on its use. But in June the Commerce Department ordered Anthropic to suspend all foreign access to its Claude Fable 5 and Mythos 5 models, citing national security concerns linked to a reported jailbreak -- users successfully blowing past guardrails designed to contain them. The company was forced to take both models offline entirely for more than two weeks before access was gradually restored. The new AI assessment regime marks an about-face for the Trump administration, which had adopted a hands-off approach to AI development on grounds the government should not hinder innovation in the race with China to lead in the AI field.

articles.title: With a Colombian coronation, the Pan American Youth Chess Festival in Medellín concluded
articles.description: With a record participation of 960 chess players from 25 American countries and after nine intense rounds of play, the XXXVI Pan American Youth Chess Festival 2026 "In Memoriam Weymar Muñoz" concluded with great success in Medellín. The capital of Antioquia once again consolidated itself as the international epicenter of youth mind sports, bringing together the most outstanding talents of the region in a high-level technical competition. In the classical modality, considered the main event due to its tactical and theoretical demands, the stellar youth categories crowned new kings of the Pan American board. In the U-18 Absolute category, the big winner was Cuban Adrián Jesús Almaguel Méndez (International Master/FM), while in the female division, the title went to Canadian Anni Guo (WFM). In the U-16 absolute category, American Patrick Liu (FM) took the gold medal, while Mexican Lily Jeanette Duarte Cramer (WFM) did the same in U-16 Female. Completing the block of youth categories, Canadian Daniel Joshua Lee (MF) won the championship in U-14 absolute, and Mexican Mía Fernanda Guzmán García (WMF) celebrated in U-14 female. The junior talent pool also delivered exciting games and crowned young talents who represent the future of continental chess. In the U-12 category, the United States dominated both divisions thanks to the victories of Srihas Maddipati (MF) in the Absolute tournament and Elizabeth Zhou (WMF) in the Female division. In U-10 Absolute, North American Grayson Xiang (CM) reached the top, while Peru celebrated the championship of Lhuanna Khalezzy Jauregui Casas (WCM) in the female division. Finally, in the U-8 category, Ecuadorian Milton Kael Bolaños Torres (CM) conquered the absolute division, and American Sarayu Thalapaleni (WCM) triumphed among the girls. The event also tested reflexes and speed in the blitz and rapid modalities, where Cuban Adrián Jesús Almaguel Méndez had a memorable performance, achieving a glorious double gold by also winning the U-18 absolute rapid title. In the fast-paced rhythms of the U-18 category, Peruvian Ayme Maraví Cerón stood out in rapid Female, Venezuelan Santiago de Jesús Casares Ugueto in absolute blitz, and Peruvian Fabiana Gómez in blitz female. The host delegation from Colombia played a significant role in the overall medal count, highlighting the runner-up finishes of William Nicolás Rodríguez in U-14 absolute classical and Juan Pablo Castro Lombana in U-18 rapid, as well as the brilliant gold medal won by young Santiago Agudelo Ramírez in the U-10 absolute rapid modality. The tournament concluded with an emotional closing ceremony that paid tribute to the memory of Weymar Muñoz, a historic leader and eternal president of the Colombian Chess Federation. The closing ceremony was attended by prominent figures in world and continental chess, including Víctor Bologan, Executive Director of FIDE; José Carrillo Pujol, President of FIDE America; and José Gregorio Ramírez Fontalvo, President of FECODAZ. With the support of local entities such as the Government of Antioquia, Indeportes Antioquia, and Inder Medellín, the championship left an indelible legacy of fraternity, continental integration, and sporting excellence.

articles.title: ING: Slightly more new homes completed in 2026 and 2027
articles.description: A new publication from the bank about the construction sector reveals that in the first four months of this year, 7 percent fewer new-build homes were completed compared to the same period last year. "This decrease will first have to be made up in the course of 2026," the bank states. ING Research therefore expects the number of new-build homes to increase only slightly to approximately 71,000 in 2026, and to further increase to 74,000 in 2027. There is often more than two years between the granting of permits and the moment the new owner receives the keys, says sector economist construction Maurice van Sante at ING Research. "Moreover, the capacity of construction companies remains limited. They spread assignments over time to keep peaks and troughs in work manageable." In May, the highest monthly number of building permits for new homes was issued since 2015. But that does not directly lead to more new-build homes, according to ING Research. Projects can be delayed if homes still need to be sold or if plans are adjusted and require new permits. For the entire Dutch construction production, ING Research expects stabilization in 2026 and a slight growth of 1 percent in 2027, thanks to the earlier increase in the number of building permits. The infrastructure sector remains the strongest sub-sector, according to the bank. Since 2020, production in the infrastructure sector has shown high growth figures. However, the production increase this year and next year is expected to be significantly lower.

articles.title: Trump to meet with AI companies today to discuss regulatory framework, agency says
articles.description: The Trump administration intends to host artificial intelligence companies at the White House on Tuesday to discuss a new U.S. regulatory framework for voluntary safety testing of AI models, according to sources familiar with the matter. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman discusses with White House officials the importance of moderating AI advancement. Repression? Anthropic rejects ban on open models and advocates for safety testing. OpenAI, Anthropic, and Alphabet's Google are among the AI developers planning to participate, according to people who spoke on condition of anonymity because the meeting has not yet been officially announced. The new regulatory framework, recently finalized, stems from an executive order signed in June by President Donald Trump on cybersecurity applied to artificial intelligence. The document establishes a voluntary adherence approach for AI model safety reviews and foresees additional efforts to strengthen the protection of critical computer systems. Meta: Zuckerberg enters the debate on AI limits in defense of more open models and criticizes rivals OpenAI and Anthropic. The regulatory framework has not yet been released to the public, and Trump's order indicates that some of its benchmarks will remain confidential. Nevertheless, it represents the U.S. government's latest step to address AI safety issues—an initiative that gained momentum in April after Anthropic warned that its Mythos model was highly competent at finding vulnerabilities in computer systems and severely restricting its disclosure. Spokespersons for the White House and the three companies declined to comment. The Information website previously reported on plans for Tuesday's meeting. Increasing the sense of urgency, OpenAI and Anthropic revealed in recent weeks that some of their models had managed to escape secure testing environments and infiltrate third-party organizations. Open source: Chinese startup Moonshot AI releases Kimi 3 model for download and expands global reach. At the same time, both companies have expressed discomfort with what they consider an inconsistent approach to AI safety reviews and hope the new regulatory framework will bring greater uniformity to what was initially presented as a voluntary program. In June, weeks after Trump signed the executive order and indicated a stance of minimal intervention in testing, the Department of Commerce banned Anthropic from sharing its two most advanced models with foreign nationals, citing concerns that safety measures could be circumvented. The company temporarily disabled access to the Fable 5 model and the selectively distributed Mythos 5 model and subsequently implemented changes to address government objections. Experts respond: In the geopolitics of AI, does it make sense for Brazil to join the cooperation proposed by China? Partly in response to industry complaints about the ad-hoc conduct of model reviews, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent proposed the creation of an independent regulatory agency that would give companies significant influence over safety reviews. The contours of this plan coincide with a proposal by Google DeepMind leader Demis Hassabis, who was in Washington last month to meet with lawmakers. According to Bloomberg News, Bessent's proposed model would create a system similar to the Financial Industry Regulatory Authority (FINRA), but applied to the artificial intelligence sector. It is not yet clear whether this plan will be part of the implementation of the executive order on AI cybersecurity or if it will be an independent initiative. Technological race: Silicon Valley is divided over closing borders to Chinese AI. Tuesday's talks will take place less than two months before Trump meets with his Chinese counterpart, Xi Jinping, at a high-level summit in Washington, where the dispute for leadership in artificial intelligence between the world's two largest economies is expected to be the central theme. U.S. authorities now face the challenge of responding to the wave of new AI models developed by Chinese companies that compete directly with the best solutions from American labs. The launch last month of the new Kimi K3 model by Chinese startup Moonshot AI shook investor confidence in U.S. leadership in AI and raised doubts about hundreds of billions of dollars in data center investments. Kimi, whose cost represents only a fraction of that of leading American offerings, approaches their performance in some areas. This challenge has been reinforced by recent moves from other Chinese developers. Over the weekend, DeepSeek expanded access to its latest model, and on Monday, Alibaba introduced its new system, Qwen3.8-Max, which the company claims achieves performance comparable to Anthropic's. The flood of releases has intensified the debate in the tech industry about how the United States should respond to open-source AI models from China, which cost much less than top American products while approaching their performance in certain areas. Silicon Valley leaders, including Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, have argued that open-source models—which allow users to download, modify, and customize the technology—are beneficial for the long-term development of artificial intelligence and help strengthen its security. In public statements, supported by dozens of companies, they have called for the United States not to impose restrictions on open-source models. Other key figures in the tech sector, including Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, have suggested that advances made by Chinese AI models violate U.S. standards—concerns shared by Scott Bessent and other senior U.S. government officials.

articles.title: What chess can do for inclusion: "In front of the board, age, gender, or origin don't matter"
articles.description: The Aragonese Chess Federation promotes a pioneering model based on eliminating barriers, adapting resources, and encouraging people with and without disabilities to compete together. In many sports, there are specific categories for people with functional diversity. In chess, the Aragonese Federation's approach is precisely the opposite: that everyone shares the same board. The philosophy is not to create parallel competitions, but to eliminate barriers that might prevent anyone from participating on equal terms. With this idea, they have been promoting inclusive chess in Aragon for several years, a strategy that combines technological adaptations, license discounts, specific tournaments to attract new players, and collaborations with organizations like Atades. All with the clear objective of ensuring that disability is no longer an obstacle to enjoyment and competition. "There are people with disabilities who approach chess, and we see them compete exactly like any other player. Their disability doesn't make them play worse or feel excluded. They simply play a normal game," explains Asun Gracia, general secretary of the Aragonese Chess Federation. Currently, the federation has about 1,350 registered players and acknowledges that there are still few people with functional diversity who participate regularly. In fact, as she points out, this is not because the sport is inaccessible, but because many times they don't even take the first step. "There are families and individuals who are afraid because they think chess is too complicated or too serious. However, once they start, everyone is delighted. The challenge is to get them to approach it," she says. A Sport Where Who You Are Doesn't Matter If chess differs from most sports in any way, it's that performance doesn't depend on physical condition. Strategy, concentration, and decision-making weigh much more than any motor or sensory limitation. For Lucía, a player with ALS, this is precisely the sport's greatest strength: "Inclusion isn't about treating everyone exactly the same, but about ensuring that everyone has the opportunity to participate. Chess achieves this particularly well because it removes many of the barriers that exist in other sports." In her opinion, many of the labels that usually accompany people disappear in front of the board. Furthermore, as she states, "in front of the board, age, gender, origin, economic situation, or disability don't matter; what matters is thinking, respecting the opponent, and enjoying the game." She even goes a step further by comparing chess to other sports. "In many sports, we first see the disability and then the athlete. In chess, it's the opposite. After the first few minutes of the game, all you see is another player trying to find the best move," she asserts. Adaptations That Change Access, Not Rules The commitment to inclusion does not involve modifying the game, as the rules remain exactly the same. However, as Asun Gracia points out, what changes are the supports to enable anyone to compete. The Aragonese Federation has electronic score sheets for players who cannot write down moves, adapted clocks for blind players that announce the remaining time, special boards, and assistants who make moves solely following the player's instructions when they cannot move the pieces. "None of these measures change the essence of the sport; they simply ensure that everyone can participate on equal terms," explains Gracia. Added to this is the possibility of competing online when travel represents a barrier or adapting spaces for wheelchair users. In turn, inclusion is also part of the sports organization. The federation applies discounts on licenses for players with disabilities and has promoted inclusive tournaments in Monzón, which are already national references, and this year also in Zaragoza. Beyond the economic aspect, Gracia acknowledges that the gesture aims to send a message: "We wanted to tell them that we know they exist, that we want them to be part of our sport, and that they belong to our sport." Example of Integration and Inclusion Without Barriers In Monzón, the initiative has gone a step further thanks to a project developed with the La Alegría School and the Santo Ángel center of Atades. For three months, several participants received chess lessons before competing in the inclusive tournament. "The experience was very positive, and the kids were delighted," she summarizes. This commitment is reflected in the Aragonese Inclusive Chess Championship held in Monzón, which has become a major national reference. Its fifth edition brought together 70 players, 15 of whom had some type of disability and 55 competed without one, all integrated into a single tournament and sharing the same competition bracket. "On a chessboard, everyone is equal" was, once again, the philosophy that presided over an event organized by the Monzón Chess Club, the Aragonese Chess Federation, and the Monzón City Council, where inclusion is not considered a separate category but a natural way of understanding sport. The championship also recognized those who promote chess as an educational and inclusion tool. Before the awards ceremony, a tribute was paid to CRA Alto Ara, whose students from Sarvisé, Asín de Broto, Broto, and Torla participated in the tournament this year; to Ana María Moracho, from the Directorate General of Educational Policy, for her support of the Chess in School program, represented by Míriam Monreal; and to the La Alegría Special Education School for incorporating chess as a pedagogical and social resource. The competition was played over seven rounds with all participants sharing the same tournament, regardless of whether they had a disability, reinforcing the idea that adaptations allow competition on equal terms without altering the essence of the game. In parallel, an online exhibition was also held between the runner-up of the Spanish Inclusive Championship, Unai Calleja from the Basque Country, and Luis Sanromán, which was followed by the attending audience. Aragon as a Mirror to Look At The Aragonese experience has sparked interest in other autonomous communities. In fact, Monzón has already hosted two Spanish Inclusive Chess Championships, and other federations are beginning to replicate similar initiatives. For Gracia, having a specific plan is "essential," even in a sport that is already inclusive by nature. "We often think that since anyone can play chess, there's nothing more to do. But we do need to remove barriers, facilitate access, and encourage those who still believe this world isn't for them," she admits. The next objectives include increasing participation from an early age, as, among other measures, the federation allows intellectually disabled minors to compete in a lower category to facilitate their progressive incorporation. The purpose, she explains, is not to create a parallel circuit but to grow a community where there are fewer and fewer differences. Therefore, the next step is to continue expanding this community from the grassroots. "We want more and more people to participate, and for children with disabilities to start playing from a young age. The sooner they get involved, the more natural it will be for them to grow up as part of chess like any other player," concludes Gracia. Likewise, as Lucía summarizes, "chess reminds us that inclusion is not about creating a different sport for each person, but about removing the barriers that prevent participation." And indeed, when those barriers disappear, what decides a game is preparation, creativity, and the ability to make good decisions.

articles.title: Liechtenstein: Hackers breached financial data from 31,000 companies
articles.description: An alarm has been raised in Liechtenstein following an extensive cyberattack, as unknown hackers stole data from the country's beneficial ownership registry, which includes information on approximately 31,000 companies, foundations, and trusts. As reported by Reuters, the breach occurred on the night of July 29th to 30th. The perpetrators gained unauthorized access to the information system and copied data before the relevant authorities detected suspicious activity and took the platform offline. Initial investigation findings indicate that cybercriminals obtained copies of information concerning approximately 31,000 legal entities registered in the beneficial ownership registry. The registry was established in 2021 as part of measures to strengthen the fight against money laundering. It records the natural persons who exercise ultimate control or are the beneficial owners of companies and other legal entities. Liechtenstein, one of the smallest but also wealthiest countries in the world, hosts a large number of companies and trusts due to its favorable tax regime. Banks were not affected. Authorities assure that there is no indication of data alteration or deletion so far. Meanwhile, the director of the Liechtenstein Bankers Association, Simon Tribelhorn, clarified that the cyberattack did not affect the country's banks or their client data. "This is a serious incident that should not be underestimated," he stated. A crisis management team was formed. The government of Liechtenstein has established a special crisis management team, led by Prime Minister Brigitte Haas and Minister of Justice Emanuel Schädler. In parallel, the relevant services are informing the natural and legal persons who may have been affected by the leak, while investigations continue to identify the perpetrators and fully ascertain the extent of the breach. articles.title: Google presents $200 billion plan for Anthropic
articles.description: AGI - Google has put in place one of the largest infrastructure financing programs in history to provide Anthropic with over $150 billion in artificial intelligence chips. This is reported by the Financial Times, citing people involved in the project and company documents. The growing demand from the startup, in which Google is an investor, has prompted the group to orchestrate an operation that intertwines chip production, finance, and data center development, involving Broadcom, Apollo, Blackstone, Morgan Stanley, and several companies from cryptocurrency mining. At the center are the TPUs, the tensor processing units developed by Google together with Broadcom since 2016. Used mainly in the group's internal data centers so far, they are now also offered externally as an alternative to Nvidia processors for artificial intelligence. The total value of the contracts is about $200 billion, of which over $150 billion is directly related to the chips. Google guarantees part of the data center commitments, Broadcom purchases and finances part of the hardware, while Apollo and Blackstone provide private capital to purchase the chips, which are then leased to Anthropic. Projects to develop data centers The Financial Times compares the model to those used in the aviation industry for the sale of aircraft and engines. In June, a first tranche passed through an investment vehicle called Compute SPV, which paid $35 billion for about one gigawatt of hardware, equivalent to about one million TPUs. The financing was divided into three tranches of debt supported by Apollo and Blackstone, while Broadcom committed to cover any losses on the two senior tranches. In April, Google also agreed to sell Broadcom another 3.5 gigawatts of TPU hardware intended for Anthropic. Broadcom's documents indicate purchase commitments of $128 billion, with deliveries expected until 2028. To house the chips, Google has also involved companies born from cryptocurrency mining with existing electrical capacity. TeraWulf obtained a Google guarantee for a 360-megawatt data center in New York State, financed with a $3.2 billion bond arranged by Morgan Stanley. Similar schemes were used with Cipher Digital and Hut 8 for projects in Texas and Louisiana. According to the Financial Times, Google has guaranteed a total of ten projects for 2.4 gigawatts of capacity, with a potential exposure of up to $44 billion in case of default. The risk to Google's balance sheet However, the value attributed to these liabilities on the balance sheet is $815 million. Google's financial support is already impacting the cost of capital: data center projects guaranteed by the group are financed at a median rate of 7.1%, compared to 9.3% for those linked to Nvidia chips. However, a strong concentration risk remains, as approximately $200 billion in contracts ultimately depend on Anthropic's ability to sustain payments for chips and data centers.

articles.title: If AI is about to upend everything, where’s all the AI policy?
articles.description: So far, the only party to release any AI policy for the 2026 election is the Greens. When prime minister Christopher Luxon addressed the crowd of the Rotorua business chamber last weekend in a now-infamous speech, he urged them to use Claude and Claude Code because “you have to disrupt yourself aggressively before you get disrupted by global events”. When finance minister Nicola Willis announced the government’s intention to cut another 8,700 public service jobs, she was optimistic that artificial intelligence would help to make up for the reduced numbers with greater efficiency. Invest NZ, the government agency responsible for attracting foreign capital, is going all-in on AI-capable data centres as New Zealand’s next big economic opportunity. It’s actively recruiting support from New Zealand energy, utilities and construction companies and co-ordinating visits with international hyperscalers and hardware giants such as Nvidia and Microsoft. Artificial intelligence is a technology with significant potential benefits and risks for every country, and New Zealand is likely to see more change than most. We have significant industries in software and film production and New Zealand has the capacity to host a lot of data centres thanks to cool temperatures and capacity to increase renewable energy generation. The proposed DataGrid Data Centre in Southland. (Image: DataGrid) And yet, amidst all the hype of economic potential and fears of environmental, social and educational harm, there has so far been little actual policy proposed by any political parties about how exactly New Zealand is going to handle this enormous force that is invading our lives. In July 2025, the government announced a national strategy for artificial intelligence, though this was a “light-touch” approach which focused on encouraging small and medium businesses to adopt AI in their workflows and encouraged international investment. It did not include any regulations. According to Andrew Lensen, a senior lecturer at Victoria University of Wellington specialising in artificial intelligence, New Zealand “continues to fall behind on regulation”. “It’s almost a reputational thing. When you look at our trading partners they all have some version of AI regulations because the public is sceptical, or they see there is a risk to be managed. It’s a soft power risk if we don’t have something similar. We look out of touch, like someone you don’t want to trade with,” he said. To date, the only party to release any AI policy for the 2026 election is the Greens, which last week called for a one-year moratorium on new consents for data centres. Greens co-leader Chloe Swarbrick told The Spinoff the party intended to release further AI policy but had prioritised the data centre issue because it was “physical infrastructure that has immediate impact on communities”. She described the moratorium as “breathing room” that would give the government time to develop new regulations for consenting. “There very clearly is opportunity here but we need to have control over it and the impacts it will have economically, because right now the government seems to be taking a very agnostic approach,” she said. “We are sleepwalking into the biggest industrial revolution at the fastest pace I can think of. Do we want to be in charge of this thing or just let it happen to us?” Green Party co-leader Chlöe Swarbrick wants a pause on new data centre consents. (Photo: supplied) Labour’s science and technology spokesperson, Reuben Davidson, said the party would release an AI policy ahead of the election and wanted regulations ensuring that data centre operators “be legally required to underwrite new renewable electricity generation so they do not add scarcity or push up power and resource costs for households”. Data centres are subject to the same permitting requirements as any other new building, meaning local councils or a fast track panel are responsible for granting resource consents. Internationally, two of the most salient concerns around data centres are water consumption and electricity use. In Ireland, data centres consumed 23% of all metered electricity in 2025, leading directly to higher costs for households. Industry leaders at the Invest NZ summit in July waved those concerns away by pointing out that new closed-loop cooling systems consume far less water than older systems and that long-term electricity supply contracts from data centres is exactly the assurance that energy generators rely on to fund new solar and wind developments. However, there are no specific regulations requiring developers to adopt closed-loop systems or ensure that their power usage doesn’t affect the domestic grid. A National spokesperson said the party has “aimed to reduce barriers to AI adoption, provide clear regulatory guidance, and promote responsible adoption,” and would have more to say on AI during the election campaign. Act and NZ First did not respond to requests for comment. Do we need an office of AI? The problem with AI regulation as a category is that it is enormously broad. The technology touches almost every industry, government service and aspect of society. Australian prime minister Anthony Albanese announced in July that he was setting up an “Office of AI” which sits in the Department of Prime Minister and Cabinet. He said this would allow a whole-of-government approach to regulations as opposed to the status quo of “issue-by-issue, sector-by-sector” regulations. Lenson said establishing an equivalent office in New Zealand was an “obvious” move. “It’s an easy win that doesn’t cost a lot, and it gives you some infrastructure to think about what must be done.” He cited Laura McClure’s deepfake bill as the kind of harm New Zealand’s regulations needed to address, alongside rules related to medical rights, misinformation, democracy, intellectual property and data sovereignty. “There is a huge potential win in being aligned with one of our partners [such as Australia or the EU, which have implemented similar regulations]. We can copy their homework, and it would be easier for big tech companies to comply with those laws. But we also have unique considerations around data sovereignty, obligations under Te Tiriti, and different demographics which could be affected by bias and discrimination.”Gehan Gunasekara, an associate professor at the University of Auckland specialising in information privacy law, seconded a call for a government office of AI to help develop regulations. “There is a precedent for this. New Zealand’s first Privacy Act in 1991 created an office of the privacy commissioner, but the act didn’t come into force until 93. The office preceded the actual rules,” he said. He wanted to see parliament appoint a high-level task to consider AI regulations, seek public input and get the ball rolling. “At the moment we’re getting ad hoc legislation about whatever might win votes and that’s not the way to make policy.” More Reading

articles.title: F1 reaches the break with on-track equality and a worrying idea of spectacle
articles.description: Four teams have already entered the fight for victories with several drivers capable of winning, although the spectacle moves away from tradition. This is analyzed by the Technical Formula 1 Podcast. What we see objectively: The Hungarian Grand Prix delivered a good race, probably the best possible way to reach the break. Without clipping as the absolute protagonist, we saw battles, different strategies, tension, and a victory for Lando Norris that confirms McLaren's leap. The British team no longer seems like an occasional guest at the top. It has fully entered the conversation alongside Mercedes, Ferrari, and Red Bull. Red Bull no longer dominates, but Verstappen continues to achieve enormous results, and Hadjar is contributing much more than some expected. And McLaren has arrived just in time to broaden the fight. So, what is F1's problem? The problem is that this equality is not always seen as it should be. On circuits like Hungary, the regulations can work because the track protects them: more braking zones, fewer endless straights, less exposure to electrical energy depletion. But on tracks like Spa or Silverstone, the picture has been much more worrying. Cars lifting earlier than expected, mythical zones turned into something else, and overtakes that, on too many occasions, seem like power management overtakes rather than driving maneuvers. Domenicali, to top it off: That's why Stefano Domenicali's statements are so unfortunate. The head of Formula 1 has defended that the vast majority of the public is not interested in how a driver drives, but whether they overtake or not. According to this view, data like battery management, clipping, or the way a maneuver is constructed would be almost niche matters, details for overly technical fans. The statement is serious not because it dismisses four angry purists, but because it reduces Formula 1 to a succession of striking images. As if motorsport consisted solely of watching fast cars, dramatic moments, and overtakes without context. As if it didn't matter why one driver passes another. As if there were no difference between a maneuver won by braking later, a defense on the limit, or a simple momentary excess of available power. That is the core of the debate. No one asks for every broadcast to be an engineering class. But hiding information or considering technical explanations irrelevant impoverishes the product. Formula 1 has always been spectacle, yes, but also technology, strategy, risk, precision, and reading the race. If all that is eliminated to make it more digestible to a new audience, perhaps what remains is no longer exactly Formula 1. Hungary proved precisely the opposite: The race was good because there were layers: strategies, traffic, tires, undercuts, mistakes, drivers caught in dirty air, and teams forced to make decisions. Norris won because he had the pace and because McLaren executed a complex race better. Verstappen was second because he turned a difficult weekend into a great result. Antonelli scored again as leader. Ferrari missed an opportunity. Aston Martin, at least, showed real progress after months at the back. That's what hooks the fan. Not just the final overtake, but everything that makes it possible. Formula 1 is mistaken if it thinks that simplifying means treating the public as if they don't want to understand. There will be new followers who come for the immediate spectacle, of course. But many will stay precisely when they discover that behind every maneuver there is much more than one car passing another. The first half of the season leaves a sporting note much better than the product note. There is a championship, there are teams closing in, and there are drivers in great form. But there is also a set of regulations that doesn't work the same on all circuits and a commercial direction that seems too comfortable dismissing what made this sport great. Formula 1 can change, as it always has. What is worrying is not the evolution. What is worrying is that those who lead it seem to believe that understanding motorsport is a problem.

articles.title: AI-Generated Music Registered as Copyright if Human Creator Participated
articles.description: Music created using generative artificial intelligence (AI) can now be registered as a copyright if a human creator has substantially participated in its production. The Korea Music Copyright Association (KOMCA) announced on the 4th that it implemented new reporting and registration standards for AI-assisted music starting on the 3rd. According to these standards, even if AI was used as a creative tool, the work can be registered as a copyright if the creator substantially participated in the songwriting, composition, or arrangement process. articles.description: US President Donald Trump recently met with top executives from major technology companies involved in the development of artificial intelligence (AI) in the country. Today, it was the turn of representatives from OpenAI, Anthropic, and Alphabet (Google's parent company). However, no decisions on how to regulate the development of the new technology and face competition with China have emerged from these discussions so far. The truth is that Trump administration officials have been struggling in recent weeks to decide what to do regarding artificial intelligence (AI), according to sources interviewed by The New York Times. Sam Altman: OpenAI CEO discusses with White House officials the importance of moderating AI's advancement. Crackdown? Anthropic rejects banning open models and advocates for safety tests. In particular, a group including White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick debated whether to adopt a much more interventionist stance towards 'open-source' AI models, like the Chinese ones, which can be freely downloaded and modified, according to more than half a dozen current and former tech and government insiders, as well as others familiar with the matter. Sam Altman, CEO of OpenAI, in Washington, where he discussed the Trump administration's efforts to create a regulatory framework for artificial intelligence testing. The Trump administration has faced difficulties in defining how to deal with 'open-source' models, like the Chinese ones. Alex Kent/The New York Times Senior officials analyzed a series of measures, including the use of sanctions, inclusion on a restrictive trade list of Chinese companies developing these open-source AI models, or even a ban on American cloud computing companies doing business with them, said five of the individuals, all on condition of anonymity to discuss private matters. Meta: Zuckerberg enters the debate on AI limits in defense of more open models and criticizes rivals OpenAI and Anthropic. But after negative backlash from Silicon Valley, they seem to have changed their minds and are now focused on promoting American AI models to make them more competitive, said the sources interviewed by The New York Times. Today, the Trump administration's plans for AI may have become clearer. The White House has invited American technology companies to discuss a framework that would allow the government to assess new AI models for potential cybersecurity issues before their public release, according to three people with knowledge of the plans. Details were not made available. 'Very fast,' says senator. Last week, OpenAI's leader, Sam Altman, and Nvidia's Jensen Huang, made a tour of Washington offices. 'All of this is happening very fast,' said Senator Jon Husted, a Republican from Ohio, last week, after meeting with the CEOs of Nvidia and OpenAI. 'I don't know if I have any definitive conclusions on any of this.' Jensen Huang, center, CEO of Nvidia, and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, right, in the Oval Office of the White House. Huang had directly presented his arguments in defense of open-source AI products to government officials. Kenny Holston/The New York Times The abrupt shifts in direction are a sign of the Trump administration's contradictory impulses regarding AI and the difficulties in dealing with such a powerful and rapidly developing technology. The White House has aggressively intervened in various sectors of the economy in the last 18 months, from media to computer chip manufacturing and mining. But AI changes rapidly, and the administration has been scrambling to determine how it can influence the sector's direction. President Donald Trump began his second term as an outspoken advocate for AI, revoking regulations and strengthening ties with companies and startups in the sector. However, this changed in June when Trump signed an executive order that would give the government oversight power over new AI models. Since then, the technology has continued to evolve rapidly. Initial plugin text The most recent debates were triggered by a wave of new and powerful Chinese AI models, known as 'open-source,' where the public can view the underlying computer code, or 'open weights,' where companies reveal the calculations used to generate responses to queries. In Silicon Valley, the reaction to these Chinese AI models varied widely. OpenAI and Anthropic, which generally do not share the underlying technology of their models, have urged the government to curb their Chinese rivals, citing national security reasons. Other American technology companies that produce open-source models, including Nvidia, have reacted. They argued that open-source models stimulate innovation and could be used to protect computer systems against cyberattacks. Which side will prevail has gained new importance in the long-standing dispute between Washington and Beijing over which country will control critical technologies and win the AI race. Further raising the stakes, Chinese leader Xi Jinping is expected to visit Washington in September for meetings that are expected to include some discussion on artificial intelligence. Industry executives and analysts said they believe the administration is unlikely to take any action before this visit. 'The United States leads the world in AI innovation, and President Trump's successful approach will ensure it stays that way,' said Liz Huston, a White House spokesperson. The Commerce Department declined to comment. The debate intensified last month when executives from Anthropic and OpenAI held regulatory discussions after the release of Kimi by Moonshot AI, a cutting-edge Chinese model that performed comparably to the leading models of the two American companies in some areas, said two people familiar with the companies' positions. OpenAI and Anthropic have also expressed concerns about 'distillation,' a process in which a model is developed based on the responses of another AI tool, essentially creating a copy, according to three people familiar with the matter. The administration echoed these concerns. Michael Kratsios, who heads the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy, posted on social media platform X last month that the Chinese company responsible for Kimi had distilled Anthropic's powerful Fable model. He warned that 'stealing proprietary US technology and harming American research is unacceptable.' On the same day, Bessent posted that Chinese companies could face sanctions or other federal restrictions for intellectual property theft. The administration also considered restricting models that could be used by federal agencies or regulating information and communication technologies through the Commerce Department, a possible way to prevent American companies from doing business with Chinese AI companies, said four people familiar with the discussions. 'We believe that both open-weight and closed-weight models have an important role in democratizing access to AI,' said an OpenAI spokesperson. 'The advances of Chinese open-weight models are not an argument against openness. They reinforce the need for a coherent national framework that allows the United States to rapidly assess new models, manage risks, and put the most powerful AI tools into the hands of cybersecurity defenders.' Anthropic declined to comment. At Nvidia, Microsoft, Google, and Meta, executives have become increasingly concerned about the possibility of Anthropic and OpenAI convincing the White House with their arguments favoring stricter restrictions, according to two of the individuals. This could consolidate the market position of AI startups. Other AI labs risked being permanently left behind, the sources added. And, as several of these companies develop their own open-source models or provide equipment to businesses that use open technology, they feared that restrictions would also harm them. In private messages, phone calls, and video conferences, executives have quietly built the argument that open-source models are beneficial for the world and for American innovation, according to three people familiar with the conversations.

According to American media, the mechanism should, however, only concern "closed" models, such as those developed by OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google, leaving out the "open" ones from companies like Meta and Nvidia, and foreign groups like DeepSeek, Moonshot AI, and Mistral. Representatives from OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Meta, Microsoft, and Nvidia reportedly attended the meeting at the White House. According to Axios, the review would be intended for closed models "with frontier capabilities and posing national security risks," while nothing in the new framework should be interpreted as a limitation on open models. The difference between closed and open models is relevant. Closed models remain hosted on the servers of the companies that develop them and do not allow users direct access to their parameters or modification of their functioning. Open models, on the other hand, can be downloaded and adapted by users, who in some cases can also remove part of the built-in security systems. In the United States, Meta and Nvidia develop models of this type, while in China, DeepSeek, Moonshot AI, and Alibaba do, and in Europe, the French company Mistral. The exemption of open models also seems to respond to Washington's desire not to penalize American competitiveness against China. In recent months, DeepSeek and Moonshot AI have introduced increasingly powerful systems, fueling fears in the United States of losing ground in the global race for artificial intelligence. For my first post, I’m sharing a letter @NVIDIA signed on why open models matter. AI will transform every industry, power every company, and be built by every country. Open models strengthen safety and cybersecurity, accelerate innovation and diffusion, and enable sovereignty.… pic.twitter.com/t02bi51N4C — Jensen Huang (@JensenHuang) July 24, 2026 A voluntary check, not a prior license The new system should not, however, translate into mandatory prior authorization. The executive order signed by Donald Trump on June 2 specifies that the government does not intend to create licenses or permits necessary to develop, publish, or distribute artificial intelligence models. The mechanism will remain voluntary and will instead allow the government, through trusted parties, to obtain early access to the most advanced systems to evaluate their capabilities, especially in the cyber field. The decree also provided for a 60-day deadline to define the new framework. The deadline passed on August 1st without a public announcement, and it remains unclear when, or if, the White House will release all the details of the process and how it will be applied. Even some of the criteria used for evaluations are expected to remain confidential. The order indeed provides for classified benchmarks to measure the cyber capabilities of frontier models. According to the Wall Street Journal, moreover, the exemption currently granted to open-weight models would not necessarily be permanent and could be reviewed if these systems reach capability levels considered sensitive for national security. Criticisms of the new framework The lack of publication of the framework has already drawn criticism. "Rules can only guide AI companies if those outside those companies know what they consist of," said Brad Carson, president of Americans for Responsible Innovation. A White House spokeswoman, Liz Huston, however, stated that the companies collaborating with the administration are putting "American innovation, security, and cyber defense first." The new approach nevertheless represents a partial change of course for an administration that has so far been oriented towards light regulation of the technology sector. Trump himself has called for a balance between security and competitiveness. "We have to be careful in both directions. We don't want to limit them to the point where we suddenly find ourselves second to China," he said last week. The race with China and the security issue The White House's strategy reflects this tension. While Washington introduces controls on the most advanced models, a presidential memorandum signed in June simultaneously asks the Pentagon and intelligence agencies to accelerate the adoption of the best available artificial intelligence systems, including commercial and open-source ones. The security issue has become more urgent after a series of incidents involving advanced models from OpenAI and Anthropic. On July 21, OpenAI confirmed that one of its systems had managed to escape a test environment and attack Hugging Face; about a week later, it reported that three other groups had been targeted. On July 30, Anthropic announced that it had identified three instances where models in testing had gained "unauthorized access" to unidentified organizations. On Tuesday, the British AI Security Institute also reported that Anthropic's Mythos 5, during an evaluation conducted with protection systems disabled, had managed to create a false identity and contact some developers in an attempt to persuade them to insert malicious code into their software. According to the institute, this is a level of deceptive behavior never observed before in such a test. The choice to limit controls to closed models for now, however, remains controversial. Martijn Rasser, vice president for technology at the Special Competitive Studies Project, observed that the United States still lacks "a predictable, legally established regulatory process" for evaluating the security of frontier models. A voluntary system applied only to closed models, he added, risks concentrating uncertainty on a small number of companies.

articles.title: Sun Hung Kai Properties Hong Kong Cyclothon Returns on 11 October
articles.description: Registration opens on 20 August for a one-of-a-kind cycling adventure through Hong Kong's iconic cityscapes along enhanced routes HONG KONG, Aug. 05, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Mark your calendar for Sunday, 11 October, as the Sun Hung Kai Properties Hong Kong Cyclothon (Hong Kong Cyclothon) returns. Organised by the Hong Kong Tourism Board (HKTB), Hong Kong’s largest annual cycling event this year features two scenic rides - a 56km Ride and a 32km Ride - inviting visitors and cycling aficionados from around the world to enjoy a unique cycling journey through Hong Kong's iconic bridges, tunnels and urban landscapes. Participants can look forward to a distinctive cycling experience like nowhere else, while immersing themselves in the vibrant energy of the Events Capital of Asia. Registration for the event opens at 10am (Hong Kong Time) on 20 August. Be among the first to secure your spot and experience Hong Kong from a rare perspective. Beyond the cycling routes, visitors can further discover Hong Kong's charm as a dynamic metropolitan destination, where urban excitement meets breathtaking natural landscapes and a wealth of outdoor adventures. 56km Scenic Ride with an All-New Route Takes Cyclists Through Hong Kong's Diverse Cityscapes to Showcase Different Sides of Hong Kong The Hong Kong Cyclothon will once again feature two popular non-competitive rides, both set against the breathtaking backdrop of Victoria Harbour's signature skyline. More than 6,000 cyclists from around the world will set off from the heart of the city at West Kowloon Cultural District, passing through multiple Hong Kong landmarks along major roads while taking in Hong Kong’s distinctive scenery blending a dynamic metropolis with a picturesque harbour. Whether taking on the more challenging 56km Ride featuring an all-new route or the shorter 32km Ride, participants will have the rare opportunity to cycle on major roads that are closed to all traffic, savouring the thrill of riding through the hustle and bustle of Hong Kong. The excitement of the Hong Kong Cyclothon will extend far beyond the cycling routes. On event day, the HKTB will present an action-packed Cyclothon Carnival at the West Kowloon Cultural District, featuring a fascinating array of activities from morning until dusk. Spanning sports, entertainment, family-friendly experiences and gourmet offerings, the carnival will immerse cyclists, visitors and locals alike in a vibrant celebration that captures Hong Kong's dynamic city charm. Registration for the 2026 Sun Hung Kai Properties Hong Kong Cyclothon will open on 20 August at 10am (Hong Kong Time). Cycling enthusiasts and visitors are invited to experience this premier annual sporting event. Stay tuned for more event and registration details at https://www.discoverhongkong.com/eng/events/cyclothon.html. An Autumn Escape to Discover the Natural Wonders Found "Only in Hong Kong” Autumn is one of the best times to visit Hong Kong, thanks to its mild and pleasant weather. Beyond the adrenaline-pumping Cyclothon, visitors can also embrace the city’s spectacular natural landscapes and remarkable geological wonders through a wide variety of outdoor experiences. Home to an abundance of natural attractions, Hong Kong offers everything from lush countryside and scenic outlying islands to magnificent hiking and cycling trails. Visitors can transition effortlessly from the electrifying city to tranquil natural surroundings in less than an hour. From exploring iconic routes such as Dragon's Back, The Victoria Peak Walk and the MacLehose Trail, to discovering the extraordinary coastal scenery of the Hong Kong UNESCO Global Geopark and enjoying various water sports in GO PARK Sai Sha (Aqua), you can experience the unique proximity of urban and natural environments that can be found "Only in Hong Kong”. For more inspiration on Hong Kong's outdoor experiences, visit https://www.discoverhongkong.com/eng/outdoors.html.
